items.title: RT Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF): Statement: Proposed withdrawal of safe harbour under Section 79 5 November 2026 The Internet Freedom Foundation ...
items.description_html:
RT Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF)
Statement: Proposed withdrawal of safe harbour under Section 79

5 November 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation is alarmed by the Indian Express that the Ministry of Electronics and IT has begun discussions on stripping social media platforms of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000. Nobody should mistake this for a move against Big Tech for it is a move against the people who use these platforms.

Safe harbour is not a gift to Meta, Google or X. It is the legal foundation that lets ordinary Indians speak online without a platform's lawyers deciding in advance whether their post is worth the risk and taking it down. If it is taken away, and every platform becomes liable for every post, comment and video. The rational response for any company is to remove anything that might draw a complaint, a notice or a summons. Criticism of the government, reporting on protests, satire, and the speech of people without lawyers will be the first casualties which are already being censored by automated filters implemented pursuant to the IT Rules, 2021. The Supreme Court recognised exactly this in Shreya Singhal (2015), which is why it read down Section 79(3)(b) to require a court order or a lawful government direction before platforms must act.

The timing tells its own story as the report says that MEITY’s rethink was shaped by a view within government that platform algorithms have favoured Opposition and anti-establishment narratives over official messaging, and by the role of Instagram during the student protests in July. In other words, the complaint is not that platforms host too much illegal content but it is that they host too much content the government dislikes.

This is also the latest step in an escalation that has been building for years. The 2023 Fact Check Unit amendment tried to make the government the arbiter of truth about itself, until the Bombay High Court struck it down. The Sahyog portal has turned Section 79(3)(b) into a parallel, opaque takedown channel that sidesteps the safeguards of Section 69A, a practice X is now challenging in court. In August, a Parliamentary Standing Committee gave Mark Zuckerberg three days to apologise personally for the brief removal of the Prime Minister's video or face the loss of safe harbour.

Subsequently advisories were issued on October 8, 2026 and October 10, 2026 pressuring digital platforms to implement pro-active censorship through, “enhanced due diligence”. Safe harbour was never meant to be a bargaining chip that MEITY waves at a company to extract compliance.

There are real problems on these platforms such as child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery and deepfakes. The Supreme Court's observations in Just Rights for Children Alliance on October 15 deserve a serious answer. But the answer is targeted, rights-respecting obligations with independent oversight, transparency about takedowns, and a grievance process that works for users. It is not a liability regime that pushes platforms to delete first and never ask. Nor is it a rule that platforms must clear product changes with the government before shipping them, which would hand the state a license raj over the design of the services Indians use every day.
Any change of this scale must go through Parliament, with a published draft, a genuine consultation and a full debate. It cannot be settled in closed-door meetings between the Ministry and a handful of companies.

What IFF will do

IFF will send a detailed representation to the Ministry of Electronics and IT setting out why the proposed changes to Section 79 are unconstitutional and unworkable, and what a rights-respecting approach to platform accountability should look like. We will also write to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology.

We are filing RTI applications with MeitY seeking the minutes, agendas, attendance lists and file notings of every meeting held on the review of safe harbour, including the meetings with Meta and other platforms in July and August, and the basis for the Ministry's assessment of how platform algorithms treat government and Opposition content. The public has a right to know who is in the room when the rules of their speech are being rewritten.

We will publish what we receive, and we invite other civil society groups, journalists and platform users to join us in asking the Ministry to put any proposal to open consultation before it goes anywhere near Parliament.

items.title: RT menaka doshi: In today's India edition I write about what Trump's rout and the Democratic sweep in the US midterm elections means for India. I susp...
items.description_html:
RT menaka doshi
In today's India edition I write about what Trump's rout and the Democratic sweep in the US midterm elections means for India.

I suspect, though, the more important cue for India is why American voters turned so decisively against Trump.

People everywhere seem to be weary of the anger of polarizing politics and the relentless change brought by technologies like AI. What they want is simpler: hope of a better life — more affordability, more security and a little less disruption.

Trump has just discovered the political cost of that discontent.

It’s a message Modi should pay attention to.

items.title: RT Jukan: Today I met with a veteran investor who argued that memory stocks are not cheap even at a P/E of 3. Below is an edited version of our conver...
items.description_html:
RT Jukan
Today I met with a veteran investor who argued that memory stocks are not cheap even at a P/E of 3. Below is an edited version of our conversation.

Memory LTAs are basically meaningless. The best the LTAs being signed today can do is get customers to shoulder part of the memory makers' capex. Once prices fall, customers will gladly forfeit their deposits (prepayments) and walk away from the LTAs.

Historically, whenever prices fell more than 60% from the peak, customers broke their LTAs even after signing them.
So even if a 2027 shortage is certain and the stocks trade at a P/E of 3 on 2027 operating profit, 2028 operating profit is uncertain, which makes it hard to justify a higher valuation.

He went on to argue that even if 2028 operating profit were certain, we would still have to account for 2029 operating profit.

I pushed back and asked why the market doesn't discount TSMC the same way. Why does TSMC get such a high valuation? Wouldn't TSMC also take a big hit if the AI boom fades?

His answer: the problem was how violently memory prices rose in the first place.
If memory makers had raised prices in a healthy way like TSMC, it might be a different story. But because they hiked prices like a commodity, the market has no choice but to treat memory stocks like commodity stocks.

Even if memory makers stay in shortage through 2030, he said, the market will price in the risk of oversupply in 2031.

He closed his argument this way: even at 3x 2027 earnings, if memory prices fall in 2028 by enough to break LTAs, that 3x multiple on 2027 works out to 7.8 to 10x on 2028. So current valuations are not cheap.

items.title: Results of Neuland and Anthem should tell you all you need to know about the lumpiness of CDMO business. Why is the CDMO business lumpy? A generic pha...
items.description_html:
Results of Neuland and Anthem should tell you all you need to know about the lumpiness of CDMO business.

Why is the CDMO business lumpy?

A generic pharma company sells pills to millions of patients, so demand flows like a river. A CDMO rents out its reactors and chemists to someone else’s drug. It might have 40 clients, but a handful of molecules usually bring in most of the money. Your quarter is decided by their trial data, their inventory, and their last funding round.

Now look at how the work actually flows. A molecule needs grams in Phase I, kilos in Phase III, and tonnes only if it gets approved. Roughly 9 out of 10 drugs that enter trials never make it, so the pipeline is always churning. Production happens in campaigns: a client books your plant for a few months, you ship one big batch, then there’s silence until the next order. Revenue is booked on dispatch, so one shipment slipping by two weeks can swing a whole quarter. And when big pharma decides to burn down inventory, as it did after COVID, orders dry up even though patients are still taking the drug.

Then comes operating leverage. Reactors, clean rooms, PhD chemists, and quality systems cost the same whether the plant is full or half empty. A 15% dip in revenue can take a much bigger bite out of EBITDA. Divi’s and Laurus both rode COVID-era contracts to record numbers and then spent the next couple of years absorbing the drop. The business wasn’t broken. The base was artificially high.

So never annualise a CDMO quarter. Look at trailing 12-month or 3-year numbers. Count the molecules in Phase III, because that’s tomorrow’s commercial revenue. Track client concentration, and listen to what management says about RFPs and inquiry flow. Lumpiness isn’t a red flag. It’s the entry fee for one of the stickiest businesses in pharma: once you’re validated on a commercial drug, replacing you means a regulatory filing and often years of work.

Disclaimer: no recommendation to buy or sell. Get used to looking at 18-36month periods to judge the results of CDMO businesses.

Electrolyte is already being made in the US. But the electrolyte salts and additives that go into it are still mostly shipped from China, with one Japanese and one Korean supplier making up the rest.

So when the compliance clock starts, US cell makers can’t just switch vendors overnight. The non-FEOC pool is thin:

> 1 Japanese supplier
> 1 Korean supplier, plus 1 more trying to come online next year
> 2 Indian players currently getting qualified

That’s 4–5 credible suppliers globally, for a market China dominates today.

This is what supply chain re-alignment looks like on the ground and this is happening across a lot of other themes and industries and one of the bigger megatrends that can be there going forward.

items.title: Shortage of castings, forgings, bearings etc hitting Honeywell aerospace. -Honeywell Aerospace has a problem most companies would love to have: more d...
items.description_html:
Shortage of castings, forgings, bearings etc hitting Honeywell aerospace.

-Honeywell Aerospace has a problem most companies would love to have: more demand than it can make parts for. Backlog grew 12% in a year to $19.3 billion, and the CFO said growth this year would have been above 8%, not 4% to 5%, if supply had kept pace.

-The parts that are missing aren’t chips. They’re the old-fashioned metal parts: castings, forgings, complex machining and bearings. Of roughly 3,000 suppliers, about 70 are critical or constrained, mostly in exactly these categories.

-A casting is molten metal poured into a mould. The hardest examples are turbine blades grown as a single crystal of superalloy so they can survive gas hotter than the metal’s own melting point.

-A forging is solid metal pressed into shape, like the discs and shafts that spin at very high speed inside an engine.

-Bearings are what let those shafts spin. You can’t scale any of this the way you scale an electronics line. You need specialised furnaces and presses, certified alloys, and workers who took years to learn the craft. That’s why management says the problem is mostly on the mechanical side, and avionics and navigation recovered faster because they face fewer raw material constraints.

Why did it break?

Three things happened at the same time.

1. First, Covid drove experienced people out of the industry, and some suppliers are still dealing with labor shortages after skilled aerospace workers left during the pandemic.

2. Second, aircraft demand came back hard.

3. Third, the industry had spent a decade optimising for margins. Honeywell itself outsourced core technologies and capabilities between 2010 and 2019, and its supply base became dependent on single-source suppliers with limited capex. Outsourcing kept costs down for ten years, and now it’s capping growth.

items.title: How compounding takes place in Businesses? A co where 2020's Topline will be their FY27's PAT. Navin Fluorine’s CDMO business is the one the market h...
items.description_html:
How compounding takes place in Businesses?

A co where 2020's Topline will be their FY27's PAT.

Navin Fluorine’s CDMO business is the one the market had written off. In Q4 FY24 it did just Rs 48 crore, down 76% after molecules got deferred. In Q2 FY27, it was the company’s fastest-growing vertical, with revenue up 78% YoY to Rs 239 crore. That’s roughly 5x in ten quarters.

The story behind that jump starts fifteen years ago in a lab in England. In 2011, Navin bought 51% of UK-based Manchester Organics for £4.335 million.

The company was founded in 1996 and specialised in lab-scale, multi-step synthesis. Navin got a call option on the remaining 49%, and the promoters got a put option, exercisable after four years. Navin took the rest in October 2015.

The advantage is easiest to see if you think of CDMO as a funnel. A molecule is first made in grams for discovery, then in kilos for trials, then in tonnes if it gets approved. Manchester Organics works with innovators at that early discovery stage, and it brings deep expertise in fluorination and high-pressure chemistry. Owning it is like owning a cricket academy: you meet the players before anyone knows they’re stars.

In the same year, Navin commissioned a cGMP pilot plant at Dewas, so the molecules it met early had somewhere to scale. Dewas was then built out one plant at a time.

A multipurpose cGMP plant for CRAMS came in 2015, and the next cGMP addition started commercial production in January 2020. In 2023 the division got its own name, Navin Molecular. The real inflection came that year with a 3-year supply agreement with Fermion starting CY2025. To serve it, Navin committed Rs 288 crore to cGMP-4, a 200 KL plant built in two phases, which nearly doubles the site’s capacity to 420 m³. Phase 1 began commercial production on 31 December 2025.

The Q2 FY27 concall filled in the next chapter. Phase 2 of cGMP-4 (about Rs 125 crore) goes live by the end of Q4 FY27, and both phases are dedicated entirely to Fermion.

The $100 million FY27 target is within striking distance on order book visibility. Two pipeline molecules are moving. One has been approved in China and is on fast track for FDA approval. The other is a label expansion of darolutamide itself.

While building Phase 2, Navin built warehousing up to Phase 6 and effluent treatment up to Phase 5, so it can move to cGMP-5 quickly. Management said it will trigger Phase 5 as soon as GMP utilisation reaches 70-80%. That means three legacy plants, cGMP-4 in two phases, cGMP-5 ready to go, and room for a sixth.

On revenue, management puts the peak potential of cGMP-4’s two phases at close to 3x the capital invested, or about Rs 900-1,000 crore by FY28-29.

A 4 digit OTP has only 10,000 probabilities and with no rate limit, anyone can break the code.

Bascially, encrypting a 4 digit code with a frontend public key and forgetting rate limits is a fundamental authentication design that should have never shipped. This is avoidable by design. All this is unbelievable.

Trust in technology is extremely hard to build but takes 1 reason to deminish that.

Their 1FA login generates a OTP & sends it. It also sends a RSA public key to front end

They haven't rate limited checks, so you can offline brute force 0 to 9999 encrypted with public key & find the OTP

items.title: RT Nandakishor m: Around 3 weeks ago introduced Laya, the first open-source version of JEV, and it has reached a very large scale. Today I am open-sou...
items.description_html:
RT Nandakishor m
Around 3 weeks ago introduced Laya, the first open-source version of JEV, and it has reached a very large scale. Today I am open-sourcing a new physics-based typed decision model called Vega.
The interesting parts. It is only 800 million parameters (4B is also there), with 73k token support, image support, and surpassing many of the jev benchmarks in single-shot. Implemented an engine+adapter as a Test-Time Training Architecture.
Imagine you are giving input to the model like "ignore all previous conversations," which is called the observation, along with a question, "Is this trying to override the instructions of the model?" and your possible outcomes are YES or NO. The whole prompt is passed to an LLM/VLM (yeah, image-supported), then from the hidden layers, we can extract the observation, question, the yes and no, and last token. These will be vectors, and we can project it by multiplying with wieghts; then, first, using the observation projection, we can create a landscape with valleys; then, using the question and last-token vectors, we can initialise a ball in the valley, and using YES or NO, we can get the candidate location of the ball. Depends on the number of outcomes we create valleys; that is, here YES and NO, so 2. When the ball fall on YES valley, we get the answer. There is friction also influencing how the ball moves.
TLDR: It's like creating valleys of outcomes that we need and throwing a ball that will slow down based on friction and settle on the best outcome

items.title: RT sphinx: My slightly contrarian, slightly in-agreement view is that India doesn’t have a Shenzhen. And without a dense manufacturing ecosystem, you...
items.description_html:
RT sphinx
My slightly contrarian, slightly in-agreement view is that India doesn’t have a Shenzhen. And without a dense manufacturing ecosystem, you won’t have the seeds of hard tech.

So debating vc investment is largely moot.

Indian hard tech startups are chasing high iq problems and that’s fine…but there’s still no Indian Anker. Even simple consumer electronics like battery chargers involve incredibly complex supply chains at cost. China has hundreds of Anker copycats operating at unit economics India simply cannot match. And that gap keeps widening as China pumps out more volume.

So founders naturally gravitate toward niche areas like rockets where the problem is more about engineering brilliance than supply chain economics. I understand the ambition, but very few startups can play that game.

Indian founders could build a saas ecosystem because it didn’t require govt support or a physical industrial base. Engineers, laptops, cloud infrastructure, and global distribution were enough. Startups could emerge first and the ecosystem followed.

Minimal govt interference - minimal infra dependency.

Hard tech works in reverse. You need suppliers, tooling, factories, skilled labor and volumes before startups can compete. These things take decades to compound, and VC money cannot shortcut that process.

In saas startups created the ecosystem. In hard tech, the ecosystem has to create the startups.

India needs a Shenzhen circa 2012 before it can have its Anker circa 2016.


Ashlee Vance: Why are Indian VCs so afraid to take risk and make money?

Someone should go to India and take risk and make money.

Our story - https://www.corememory.com/p/a-new-india-is-here

items.description_html:
RT Waterfield Advisors
What does it really take to invest like a professional?

In our latest episode of Capital Conversations, @SamitVartak, Founder & CIO of SageOne Investment Managers, joins us for a masterclass on investing like a professional.

Drawing on over 14 years of experience, Samit shares how he built a strong track record across strategies by focusing on high-quality small and mid-cap businesses.

Some key takeaways:

i. How early mistakes shape your approach to risk.
ii. Why bottom-up, sector-agnostic investing outperforms consensus-driven stock picking.
iii. The three ingredients of a multi-bagger: low valuations, strong earnings growth, and the discipline to hold.
iv. Why rebalancing, cutting losses quickly and protecting capital matter in downturns.

🔗 Watch the full episode on Waterfield’s YouTube channel. Link in comments.

items.title: P/B ratio has historically been a more reliable and stable valuation metric for predicting future returns compared to alternatives such as P/E or EV/E...
items.description_html:
P/B ratio has historically been a more reliable and stable valuation metric for predicting future returns compared to alternatives such as P/E or EV/EBITDA. I had demonstrated this through correlation analysis in an earlier investor memo.

The chart below tracks the P/B ratio (blue line) of the Nifty Smallcap 100 Index against the 25th percentile of its trailing 5-year P/B range (orange line). In simple terms, when the blue line falls below the orange line, the current valuation is in the lowest quartile of the past five years.

Since P/B is broadly proportional to ROE, the structural improvement in index ROE—from ~8–12% in the previous decade to ~15% currently—has led to a gradual upward shift in the orange line over time.

Notably, for the first time since the COVID crash, the current P/B has moved below this 25th percentile threshold. Historically, similar instances—during the 2011–2013 downturn, Q1 2016 correction, and the COVID crash—have been followed by strong returns over the subsequent 1–3 years.

This does not imply that markets have bottomed, nor does it guarantee short-term gains. In an event-driven environment, especially with geopolitical risks such as an escalation in war, markets could decline further by 10–20%.

However, what can be said with a reasonably high degree of confidence is that forward-looking returns over a 1–3 year horizon from such valuation levels have historically been better than average.

items.description_html: In my experience, this is probably the first time the Mid & Small cap indices have outperformed the Nifty 50 during a crisis time. It's also extremely rare to see the Mid & Small cap indices (avg of the two) beating the Nifty 50 near the bottom of the cycle. Their avg CAGR has outperformed during the last two tough years as well as all the below trailing years. I am not that surprised as their balance sheet, P&L and cash flow quality has substantially improved post COVID. I believe the biggest multi-baggers will emerge from this space as the earnings growth differential will be significant going forward. Because of the quality differential today vs during pre-COVID period, I would be surprised if their valuations correct to levels seen during the previous crashes. We probably have the best corporate quality and least stressed financials currently compared to any other previous big crisis.

items.title: Sky Gold spoke about its parallels with Walmart and also explained the cost of capital/ROIC nicely. "The right test for any growth investment is simpl...
items.description_html:
Sky Gold spoke about its parallels with Walmart and also explained the cost of capital/ROIC nicely.

"The right test for any growth investment is simple: does each rupee we invest earn more than its cost of capital? If it does, investing it creates value. Even if free cash flow is lower in the near term, what matters is the spread between ROIC and cost of capital and how long we can sustain it. Consider Walmart between 1973 and 1986, the years it was building out its store network.

It had negative free cash flow in every one of those 14 years, yet its ROC averaged 18%, well above its cost of capital, and its stock returned 33% a year, about 3 times the S&P 500. Walmart was not burning cash; it was putting every dollar it could to work at high returns while the opportunity was in front of it.

We see real parallels with Sky Gold. Like Walmart then, we are early in a structural shift, in our case from unorganized to organized jewelry manufacturing. Like Walmart, our growth follows a clear demand signal"

We need to appreciate well-read promoters/mgmt. who give out detailed commentary and examples

Src- Q2FY27 concall, strictly no stock reco

items.description_html:
Dixon is building some serious scale. Two numbers from its Q2FY27 call caught my attention:

📷 Camera manufacturing:

Qutek, its 51% subsidiary and an EMS/ECMS beneficiary, operates India’s largest camera manufacturing plant.

Annual capacity has already grown from 8 crore to 12 crore units, with plans to reach 18–19 crore by the next fiscal. Deeper manufacturing is also helping margins.

🧺 Washing machines:

Dixon says it has built India’s largest manufacturing capacity:

• Semi-automatic: 30 lakh units
• Fully automatic top-load: 6 lakh
• Fully automatic front-load: 3 lakh

That’s 39 lakh units annually against India’s estimated annual requirement of 1.2 Cr - capacity equivalent to roughly one-third of the market!

Next up: dishwashers, microwaves and ovens, slated for launch in Q4 of the current fiscal.

More categories, higher capacity, and more manufacturing done in-house. The next thing to watch is how well these capacities fill up!

Src: Dixon Q2FY27 call | No reco

items.title: I was sitting over coffee with a veteran wealth banker a few days back when he made a mild quip - "NSE listing will make half of private bankers joble...
items.description_html:
I was sitting over coffee with a veteran wealth banker a few days back when he made a mild quip - "NSE listing will make half of private bankers jobless."

As this enigma called NSE lists today after more than a decade of waiting, let me explain what he meant and why this matters. It won't be wrong to say that NSE pretty much created the pre-IPO investing category in India.

NSE has over 2.3 lakh private market shareholders. Another 70-80 lakh IPO applicants would be watching the tape at 10 am today with anticipation.

Interestingly, there were only 80 shareholders in 2016 when NSE first attempted to IPO. Even as recent as 2020, the count was a paltry 310 shareholders.

Almost an 800x surge post Covid!

Let us say NSE did to private markets what Jio did to data. And NSE was to private Wealth bankers what ULIP was to LIC agents :)

Suddenly, you did not need to be a PE fund in Singapore. Or on a VVIP list. You just needed a demat and a relationship manager who could whisper - “I can source a small lot.”

The Banker did not have to explain the company. The client already used it every trading day. Institutions sold, employees sold ESOPs, HNIs bought, then sold to the next HNIs. The round robin continued each year. Every transfer paid a spread - pocketing the Wealth house a sweet a 2-3% each time the stock changed hands. This is huge for an industry that makes just 30-40 bps on all Assets under Management.

As per UnlistedZone, NSE was half of all unlisted volume in India between 2023 and 2025!

The continued delay of a large, liquid, hot asset was the private bankers dream. It was demand-supply matched inventory.

Today that inventory lists - only on BSE, and not on its own boards. About ₹22,560 crore of pure Offer for Sale. The business doesn't need cash.

NSE created the pre-IPO market for likes of Tata Capital, SBI AMC, Swiggy, NSDL, Lenskart, etc. It created a category.

I don't think the veteran Banker was predicting pink slips. But I do think he was indicating the end of easy money for Wealth managers. The industry has turned a lot more competitive and the incentives are a lot more elusive + you hope for some luck. The money is now in the long run and business economics might have to readjust.

Wealth bankers will still do advice, credit, estate, "the ego massage" and the work of stopping a family from doing something stupid.

What ends today is the easy door-opener. For ten years NSE was that door. From today, it is a ticker.

#NSEIPO

items.title: RT Parimal: In 2014, India made less steel than Japan. In 2025, India made more steel than the US and Japan put together. Read that again. 87 million ...
items.description_html:
RT Parimal
In 2014, India made less steel than Japan.

In 2025, India made more steel than the US and Japan put together.

Read that again.

87 million tonnes in 2014.
165 million tonnes in 2025.

Almost doubled in one decade. In the same decade, Japan fell 27%. The US fell 7%.

India is now the world's #2 steel producer. Only China is ahead.

And steel is not a services story / an app story. It is what a nation builds with railways, bridges, factories, ships, guns. The countries that ruled the 20th century were the countries that made the most steel.

The strange part? Nobody is talking about this. Just one quiet line in a World Steel Association release.

Bharat is rising. 🙏🙏

Source: World Steel Association, calendar-year crude steel production data. Graph made by me.

items.title: Upfront Capital Support is the new PLI. Today, the Union Cabinet has approved up to 30% capex support for lithium and nickel processing plants. Unlike...
items.description_html:
Upfront Capital Support is the new PLI.

Today, the Union Cabinet has approved up to 30% capex support for lithium and nickel processing plants.

Unlike PLI, where support comes after production starts, upfront capital support comes in tranches as firms meet specific milestones. The same technique was used for chip fabs and chip assembly plants.

What this does not yet resolve is the price-shock risk processing firms face. For that, processors will have to lock in long-term purchase agreements with price-floor guarantees with buyers.

Source: @PIB_India

Ask an investor why they chose a particular mutual fund, and you’ll probably hear the usual suspects – returns, risk, track record, AUM, investment philosophy. But when it comes to actually making that choice, are these really the deciding factors?

What people say they do and what they actually do can be two very different things.

At @capitalmind_in , we find questions like these fascinating. Because in the real world, the most interesting business problems rarely come with ready-made answers. And we believe some of the sharpest perspectives on these problems could come from the next generation of business leaders.

So, we’re taking a real-world business challenge beyond our boardrooms and into the classrooms of premium B-schools. An upcoming national case study competition at the intersection of Behavioural Finance, Consumer Psychology and real-world decision-making.

No rehearsed frameworks. No obvious answers. Just curiosity, original thinking and the ability to back your conclusions with evidence. An opportunity to challenge assumptions, demonstrate how you think, and get a closer look at the kind of problems we enjoy solving at Capitalmind.

To the curious minds (and the future business leaders), we have something interesting coming your way.

items.title: RT Capitalmind Mutual Fund: When we look at index returns, we generally see only how much the market has gone up or down. But that doesn't tell us wha...
items.description_html:
RT Capitalmind Mutual Fund
When we look at index returns, we generally see only how much the market has gone up or down. But that doesn't tell us what happened to earnings and valuations during that period.

Take the Nifty 500 and Smallcap 250. Both fell 7.9% between September 2024 and October 2026. But what happened underneath was quite different.

For the Nifty 500, the implied earnings component contributed positively to returns but that was more than offset by falling valuations. In small caps, both implied earnings and valuations contributed negatively.

And look at mid caps. The Nifty Midcap 150 returned just -4.5% but that small decline hides two very large movements. Implied earnings contributed a positive 48.3 percentage points while falling valuations contributed a negative 54 points. They almost cancelled each other out.

So two indices can deliver the same return even when their earnings and valuations move very differently. And sometimes a small change in an index can hide much bigger movements underneath.

So when an index falls, it's worth looking at what happened to its earnings and valuations along the way. The return alone doesn't tell us the full story.

𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗮𝘄𝗮𝘆𝘀 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗹𝘆𝘀𝗶𝘀:

We expect the FY27 fiscal deficit to exceed the budgeted amount by Rs 0.7-0.8 trillion, leading to a fiscal deficit-to-GDP of 4.3-4.5%.

However, the Centre could meet its deficit target through the Rs 1 trillion Economic Stabilisation Fund.

Customs duties and GST collections are projected to remain supportive, with tax collections exceeding budget estimates in FY27.

However, we expect lower than budgeted revenues from excise duty collections and income taxes.

Overall, we expect gross tax revenue to see a shortfall of Rs 1 trillion in FY27.

Support from higher dividend transfers and disinvestments could contain the slippage in the overall receipts to Rs 0.5 trillion.

On the spending front, we expect the subsidy burden to rise by Rs 1.2 trillion, which could be partially offset by some revenue rationalisation and marginally lower capex.

Overall, we expect the total expenditure to exceed the budgeted target by Rs 0.3 trillion.

CareEdge Ratings’ latest analysis points to a notable divergence in market activity.

Key takeaways:
• The Margin Trading Facility (MTF) book rose to a new all-time high of ₹1.56 lakh crore in September 2026, growing 53.3% YoY, reflecting sustained investor preference for leveraged cash-equity exposure.
• The F&O segment recovered sequentially, with trading activity stabilising as market participants adapted to regulatory changes and evolving market conditions.
• In contrast, cash-market turnover moderated, impacted by cautious sentiment, softer retail participation, and a continued shift towards derivatives.
• Looking ahead, while cash-market activity may remain sentiment-sensitive, the long-term outlook for MTF remains favourable amid rising adoption and its growing relevance for brokers.

As global growth navigates persistent inflationary pressures and elevated energy prices, India’s macroeconomic fundamentals continue to show relative strength. Yet, emerging risks warrant closer attention.

Key Takeaways:
• High-Frequency indicators tell a positive story, but risks warrant caution.
• Elevated crude oil prices, food inflation, and rising input costs are broadening inflationary pressures, with CPI inflation expected to average around 5% in FY27.
• Merchandise exports have maintained double-digit growth momentum, although higher oil and electronics imports have widened the trade deficit.
• Healthy public capex continues to support infrastructure and capital goods growth, providing an important buffer to economic activity.
• Given the current growth-inflation dynamics, the current hiking cycle will be shallow, with a further cumulative increase of 50 bps over the next few policy meetings.

Nepal’s general insurance sector is entering a critical phase as successive loss events continue to test underwriting resilience. While reinsurance and capital buffers have helped contain balance sheet stress so far, profitability has come under significant pressure.

Key takeaways:
• FY26 underwriting performance weakened as net claims incurred rose 23.3%.
• The August 2026 floods have brought concentration risk into sharper focus, with claims largely concentrated in property and engineering portfolios.
• Reinsurance quality, recoverability, counterparty diversification, and catastrophe protection are emerging as key differentiators across insurers.
• Solvency buffers remain supportive, but future resilience will depend on retention practices and timely reinsurance recoveries.

CareEdge Ratings’ latest BFSI analysis points to a cooling in banking system momentum as quarter-end gains unwound. While credit and deposit growth remain robust on a year-on-year basis, liquidity dynamics and funding costs warrant close monitoring.

Key takeaways:
• Bank credit growth eased to 18.2% YoY from 19.4% at September-end, following a post quarter-end decline in outstanding credit.
• Deposit growth moderated to 16.7% YoY, with the credit-deposit growth gap largely unchanged at 151 bps.
• The loan-to-deposit ratio rose to 81.6%, marking its third consecutive increase, indicating persistent funding pressures.
• The WACR climbed above the repo rate as surplus liquidity narrowed, signalling firmer money market conditions.
• CD issuance declined, but wholesale funding costs could remain under pressure as liquidity conditions tighten.

India’s credit card spending declined 5.9% y-o-y to Rs 2.04 lakh crore in September 2026, marking the first annual decline since February 2021. However, the fall was largely influenced by a high base and the shift of festive sales from September last year to October this year.

Key takeaways:
• Card spending fell despite a 10.5% y-o-y rise in cards outstanding, indicating slower spend intensity.
• Transactions surged 23.2% y-o-y, while average ticket size dropped 23.6%, reflecting increased usage for smaller-value payments.
• Online spending declined 12.5% y-o-y, whereas PoS spending grew 7.2%, leading to a lower online share of total spends.
• Private banks strengthened their spending share, while spending growth outside major issuers remained mixed.

Nepal’s edible oil refining industry has grown into a major export-oriented sector, but its fortunes remain closely tied to tariff differentials and policy decisions across borders. A key takeaway from our latest analysis: tariff arbitrage continues to be the primary driver of export competitiveness, making the sector highly sensitive to regulatory shifts.

Key insights:
• Recent duty reductions by India have narrowed the tariff advantage enjoyed by Nepalese refiners, potentially moderating export growth and profitability.
• Strong earnings in FY25-FY26 were supported by favourable tariff arbitrage, but margin pressures may re-emerge as the duty gap contracts.
• Inventory holding risks remain significant, particularly in a volatile commodity price environment.
• Debt servicing metrics, liquidity, and leverage will remain vulnerable if profitability weakens over a prolonged period.
• Going forward, India's import duty regime and global edible oil price movements will be critical variables to watch.

CareEdge-ESG analyses why the answer matters for India’s industrial strategy.
With the EU’s CBAM now in its definitive phase, carbon intensity is increasingly shaping market access and cost structures for steel, aluminium, fertilisers and hydrogen. For India, green hydrogen is emerging as a strategic industrial question, even as the economics remain challenging.

Key takeaways from our latest analysis:

Green hydrogen production costs in India remain 2–2.5x higher than grey hydrogen, making cost parity the sector’s biggest hurdle.

The global market faces a significant execution challenge, with projects that are operational, under construction or near FID far below announced pipelines for 2030.

For Indian steel exporters, CBAM-related carbon costs could materially influence competitiveness, strengthening the case for low-carbon production pathways.

India’s combination of policy support, low-cost renewable energy and large industrial demand creates a meaningful opportunity, provided execution keeps pace with ambition.

Private investment of $180–200 billion is expected through 2030, though announced commitments still exceed FID-backed investment.

The real question for ESG-oriented investors and industrial strategists is where value will concentrate across the value chain.

items.title: It’s not that flat oil benchmark prices crashed, perhaps more importantly the physical market sent an even stronger signal of the wave of supply. The...
items.description_html:
It’s not that flat oil benchmark prices crashed, perhaps more importantly the physical market sent an even stronger signal of the wave of supply.

The physical premium in the Middle East market (Oman vs Dubai) plunged today to almost zero (from >$30 a barrel in mid Sept). In the Dated Brent market, the physical premium for North Sea crude plunged to minus ~$1 a barrel (it was plus ~$19 in early Oct).

The physical premia in both the Middle East and North Sea markets is now the lowest in about 3 ½ months.

items.description_html:
BREAKING: US diesel inventories dropped -3.6 million barrels last week, to 99.3 million barrels, the lowest level since May 2003.

Since January 2026, distillate fuel oil inventories have declined -33.7 million barrels, or -25%.

Furthermore, the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) fell -399,000 barrels last week, to 282.2 million barrels, its lowest since October 1982.

Since March, oil inventories in the SPR have dropped by -133.2 million barrels, or -32%.

Meanwhile, commercial crude oil stocks excluding the SPR declined -865,000 barrels last week, to 409.8 million barrels, their lowest reading since July 31st.

US fuel reserves are being depleted at a rapid pace.

items.title: RT Nimesh Shah: UBS on SBI Neutral, TP Rs 1100 Reported a mixed quarter with strong NII growth of 5% QoQ and NIM of 2.94% (+8bp), both ahead of est. Y...
items.description_html:
RT Nimesh Shah
UBS on SBI
Neutral, TP Rs 1100
Reported a mixed quarter with strong NII growth of 5% QoQ and NIM of 2.94% (+8bp), both ahead of est.
Yet, loan growth of 18.2% YoY (19% in 1Q) & 3% miss on PPOP due to higher opex were key negatives
There was also a one-time gain from SBI MF listing of Rs72.9bn but was partly offset by treasury losses of Rs12.8bn.
Ex - of listing gain RoA for H1 was <1% vs reported RoA of 1.14%.
Retail loan growth of 14.5% YoY continued to lag overall loan growth and segments other than gold remained weak.
Bank continues to maintain full year guidance of 14-15% loan growth, 1% RoA and >3% domestic NIM

Macquarie on SBI
O-P TP Rs 1220
2Q: Exceptional gains aid earnings, loan growth remains healthy
Margins resilient
Asset quality remains healthy, ECL impact manageable
At 1.3x FY28E P/BV, valuations look comfortable against expected ROA above 1%.

CLSA on SBI
O-P, TP Rs 1325
Delivered a 2% NII beat versus our estimates, driven by an 11bp QoQ domestic NIM expansion.
Lower fee income and treasury losses led to a 3% PBT miss.
Domestic loans growth, at 17% YoY, was broad-based, while international loans declined 3% QoQ, adjusted for FCNR deposit-backed loans.
Deposit growth was healthy at 12% YoY, with 8% YoY CASA growth only soft spot.
In line with sector, asset quality continued to improve, with net slippages down 10bp YoY, even off a low base.
SBI should be largely unaffected by the new insurance distribution guidelines, with distribution income less than 3% of PBT.

Bernstein on SBI
Market Perform, TP Rs 1300
Headline earnings growth masked a softer underlying quarter, with lower credit costs & stake-sale gains supporting profitability.
Healthy loan growth & an 8 bps QoQ NIM recovery failed to lift underlying PPoP, which declined 1% YoY amid weaker other income and rising
expenses.
Excluding one-offs, EPS grew a more modest 5% YoY, while RoA declined 21 bps QoQ to 0.90%, compared with reported EPS growth of 13% and RoA of 1.19%

HSBC on SBI
Buy TP Rs 1220
2QFY27 underscored by strong NII / NIMs, while loan growth was lower, opex higher than estimates
Upgrade EPS by 4-8% for FY27-29e on stronger-than estimated NIM momentum and operating leverage playing out
TP cut as build in some discount for slower loan growth, lower multiples for some subsidiaries

CITI on SBI
Buy, TP Rs 1300
SBI's Rs230bn PAT (up 14% YoY) was lifted by a Rs72.9bn stake-sale gain, partly offset by a Rs12.8bn treasury loss and 15% YoY/38% QoQ opex growth.
NII rose 14% YoY/4.6% QoQ, beating estimates as NIMs expanded 8bps (vs our forecast of 2bps decline).
With 49% of loans linked external benchmarks (incl 32% repo-linked), NIMs should skew favorably in a rising-rate cycle, though management conservatively reiterated 3%+ NIM guidance. Loan growth was modest at 3.3% QoQ/18.2% YoY, lagging the system as corporate lending stayed flat.
Management retained 14-15% FY27 advances guidance, though we expect 16%+
Slippages stayed below 0.5%, credit costs under 0.35%.
ECL transition impact is pegged at Rs195bn (3.3% of net worth, 0.4% of advances).

Nomura on SBI
Neutral, TP Rs 1100
2QFY27 – NII beat, but loan growth slows
In-line core performance; weak treasury, higher opex offset by one time gain on SBI FUNDS stake sale
NIM expansion led to NII beat; higher opex, lower other income resulted in PPOP miss
Growth guidance maintained at 14-15% in FY27P; asset quality benign

Kotak Inst Eqt on SBI
Buy, TP Rs 1250
Reported 15% yoy earnings growth, led by a 7% yoy operating profit growth (stake sale in mutual fund). RoE at 15% was driven by healthy NII growth (~15% yoy), NIM recovering ~10bps qoq and a low credit cost (~30bps).
Asset quality remains a minor concern
Like franchise given its inexpensive valuation for a superior return profile.

items.title: RT Marya Shakil: BIG CLARIFICATION BY THE ELECTION COMMISSION ON FORM 6 AND SIR The ECI has clarified that voters whose names do not figure in the dra...
items.description_html:
RT Marya Shakil
BIG CLARIFICATION BY THE ELECTION COMMISSION ON FORM 6 AND SIR

The ECI has clarified that voters whose names do not figure in the draft electoral rolls can submit Form 6 for fresh inclusion — even if they were enrolled previously.

Crucially, the Commission says:

• Previous enrolment does not make the Form 6 declaration false.
• No action under Section 31 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950, can be initiated merely because the elector was previously enrolled and has submitted Form 6.
• This protection applies provided the elector is not already enrolled in another Parliamentary or Assembly constituency and the declaration is otherwise lawful.

The clarification comes amid concerns among deleted voters that submitting Form 6 could expose them to prosecution for making a false declaration. The ECI has directed Chief Electoral Officers to publicise this clarification widely.

items.title: RT Anuj Singhal अनुज सिंघल: SEBI has made KYC compliance easier for Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs). Here’s what has changed: 1. KYC revi...
items.description_html:
RT Anuj Singhal अनुज सिंघल
SEBI has made KYC compliance easier for Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs).

Here’s what has changed:

1. KYC review will happen less frequently as SEBI has increased the time gap between mandatory KYC reviews.

2. One more compliance requirement removed- FPIs will no longer have to separately confirm whether previously submitted information has changed when continuing their registration.

3. When will it take effect? : Effective December 1, 2026

Why is this important?
Less paperwork for foreign investors.
Fewer repetitive compliance requirements.
Lower administrative costs.
Easier to do business in Indian markets.
A step towards making India more investor-friendly.

The bigger takeaway
SEBI is trying to make life easier for FPIs and reduce compliance hurdles to encourage foreign investment into Indian markets.

In simple terms: Less paperwork, fewer KYC checks and easier compliance for foreign investors.

items.title: Lower Valuations Today Could Drive FII Inflows Tomorrow An interesting study by JM Financial suggests that FII flows follow valuations with a 4–5 mon...
items.description_html:
Lower Valuations Today Could Drive FII Inflows Tomorrow

An interesting study by JM Financial suggests that FII flows follow valuations with a 4–5 month lag.

Historical data from 2006–2026 reveals:

• Below 15x P/E: Average FII inflows of $18.8 billion over the next 12 months.
• 15–18x P/E: Average inflows of $14.1 billion.
• 18–21x P/E: Average inflows of $11 billion.
• Above 21x P/E: Average outflows of $4.3–4.7 billion.

Where Are We Today?
The Nifty trades at ~17.1x one-year forward P/E, placing it in a historically favourable valuation zone for FII inflows.

items.title: Susan Electricals ~ Stronger H2 FY27 Ahead, Backed By ₹347 Cr Order Visibility Susan Electricals' management expects a significantly stronger H2 FY27...
items.description_html:
Susan Electricals ~ Stronger H2 FY27 Ahead, Backed By ₹347 Cr Order Visibility

Susan Electricals' management expects a significantly stronger H2 FY27, supported by capacity expansion and growing demand for higher-value cables.

Key Management Takeaways:

• Order Visibility: ₹147 Cr confirmed order book and ₹200 Cr active pipeline, taking potential visibility to ₹347 Cr.

• CCV Line: Expected to become operational shortly, enabling participation in a wider range of HT cable projects.

• Cable Capacity: Expanding from 11,000 km to 16,000 km annually, a ~45% increase.

• Winding Wire Capacity: Increased from 3,307 to 4,200, with further expansion to 5,500 planned (~66% above the original capacity).

• Product Mix: Increasing focus on High-Tension (HT) cables and Medium Voltage Covered Conductors (MVCC).

• Balance Sheet: Operating cash flow has turned positive despite rapid business growth.

• Future Expansion: Company is in advanced stages of taking possession of newly acquired land for additional capacity.

The Bigger Picture: Susan Electricals is moving towards larger projects and higher-value products, with manufacturing expansion supporting its next phase of growth.

Key Monitorables: CCV commissioning, H2 order execution, margin recovery and conversion of the ₹200 Cr pipeline into firm orders.

RT Alter Magazine
In 2004, India’s official count said the Sariska Tiger Reserve in Rajasthan had 16-18 tigers. But, visitors had not seen one in months.

The truth: Sariska’s tigers had been poached to extinction.

What follows is the stunning story of how a supposedly, “poor country” mobilised to save the tiger. From rebuilding its counting methods, camera traps, statistics, satellites and an app.

This is the story of how a country that has learnt to lived with tigers for millennia, learnt again how to protect it.

Issue 7: How India Actually Saved the Tiger, written by @sonakshi_geog, edited by @fahadmh , tracked, counted & built by @AltCarbonIndia

items.description_html:
RT Tijori
Saudi Arabia is reducing oil cargoes to European refiners. Oil being cut off has happened to Europe before, Abqaiq (2019) and the 2022 Russia Disruption

At that time Indian refiners who benefitted massively were RIL, MRPL AND CPCL

RIL — the big direct winner. Most of what it makes is transport fuel, and the SEZ refinery is built to export.

MRPL — exports ~40% of its output, and half its slate is diesel + ATF. Exactly what Europe will be short of.

-CPCL is an indirect beneficiary. Products transferred from CPCL to parent IOCL are billed on an import-parity pricing (IPP) basis. When international product benchmarks and cracks increase, CPCL's realized refinery-gate prices rise immediately, boosting standalone GRM and operating cash flows.

items.description_html:
RT Exencial Research Partners
🚨 MORGAN STANLEY JUST FLAGGED A $250 BILLION AI RISK HIDING IN THE SOFTWARE CREDIT MARKET.

While Nomura and Bernstein highlight the enormous opportunity in AI infrastructure, Morgan Stanley reveals the other side of the boom.

And the numbers are alarming.

Morgan Stanley analyzed ~$250B of software loans:

🔴 16% HIGH AI disruption risk (~$40B)
🟡 49% Moderate risk
🟢 35% Low risk

But here's where it gets interesting:

• ~$20B of high-risk software loans already trade at distressed levels.

• Average loan prices: 97 for low-risk vs. 73 for high-risk borrowers.

• ~75% of high-risk exposure matures during 2027–2029.

• Weaker borrowers could face 550–1,000 bps in additional refinancing costs.

• Front-office applications have the highest share of high-risk loans at 32%.

These are AI vulnerability assessments, not default forecasts.

NOW CONNECT THE THREE REPORTS:

NOMURA: AI data centers are already generating substantial operating profits. Negative FCF largely reflects heavy upfront investment.

BERNSTEIN: OpenAI's infrastructure commitments may be more manageable than feared, but compute oversupply could pressure neocloud economics.

MORGAN STANLEY: AI disruption risk is already influencing software debt valuations—and refinancing pressure could intensify before earnings fully reflect disruption.

THE BIGGER PICTURE:

AI is creating extraordinary opportunities in infrastructure while threatening the economics of weaker software businesses.

The next big AI trade may not just be about who captures the billions flowing INTO AI infrastructure.

It may be about who loses pricing power, who struggles to refinance, and who gets left holding the debt.

AI isn't just reshaping technology.

It's starting to reshape credit markets.

items.description_html:
🚨 OPEC: The real oil price shock isn't just crude. It's the cost of moving it.

Shipping crude oil from the Middle East to East Asia has become dramatically more expensive in just 9 months.

OPEC's November 2026 data reveals a staggering escalation in tanker freight and insurance costs.

📊 The numbers are alarming:

VLCC freight costs:

• January 2026: $3.18/barrel
• October 2026: $37.13/barrel

🔺 Nearly 12x higher

Marine insurance costs:

• January 2026: $0.06/barrel
• October 2026: $12.29/barrel

🔺 More than 200x higher

Combined freight + insurance:

• January: $3.24/barrel
• October: $49.42/barrel

That's an additional $46.18 per barrel in transportation and insurance costs.

⚠️ Freight and insurance now account for 30% of total crude oil costs on this route, compared with just 5% in January.

A sixfold increase in their share of total costs.
OPEC also highlights a critical point:

Current disruptions to the tanker fleet explain only a small fraction of the surge in shipping costs and insurance premiums.

These elevated costs are being transmitted through the value chain, increasing expenses for oil producers and consumers while adding inflationary pressure to the global economy.

items.description_html:
RT Exencial Research Partners
🚨 BERNSTEIN JUST DROPPED A MAJOR REPORT ON THE $750 BILLION AI INFRASTRUCTURE BOOM.

After Nomura argued that AI data centers are far more profitable than investors think, Bernstein tackles an even bigger question:

Can OpenAI actually afford its massive compute commitments and who ultimately captures the profits?

The findings are fascinating:

• $750B vs. $614B: Bernstein models ~$614B in OpenAI infrastructure payments through 2030, with annual spending potentially peaking at $184B in 2031. Not every announced commitment is binding, and actual spending could be lower.

• OpenAI's revenue is catching up: Bernstein cites a ~$50B annualized revenue run rate in September 2026, growing ~77% YoY. If growth remains strong, revenue could scale faster than infrastructure obligations.

• Oracle's $300B opportunity: Capacity comes online in stages, with Bernstein estimating only ~57% of modeled OpenAI contract revenue recognized through Oracle FY2030. The backlog represents a multiyear revenue opportunity, not immediate cash generation.

• Microsoft and Amazon have structural advantages: Their integrated cloud platforms, enterprise ecosystems and AI services offer more durable economics than simply renting GPUs.

• CoreWeave faces a different challenge: Bernstein is comfortable with existing contracts but questions renewal economics once compute becomes less scarce.

• The biggest risk may be oversupply, not OpenAI defaulting. Bernstein sees potential supply-demand normalization within 2–3 years, putting pressure on GPU rental prices and weaker infrastructure providers.

HERE'S THE REAL INSIGHT:

Nomura explains why AI infrastructure can remain profitable despite negative free cash flow.

Bernstein explains why that profitability won't necessarily be distributed equally.

The first phase of the AI boom rewarded companies that could secure GPUs, power and data-center capacity.

The next phase may reward companies that control customers, platforms and pricing power.

AI demand can keep exploding while returns on undifferentiated compute infrastructure deteriorate.

Being bullish on AI infrastructure spending is NOT the same as being bullish on every AI infrastructure stock.

That distinction could define the next leg of the AI trade.

items.title: RT Exencial Research Partners: 🚨 NOMURA: THE MARKET MAY BE MISREADING THE ENTIRE AI DATA CENTER BOOM. Big Tech is spending hundreds of billions on ...
items.description_html:
RT Exencial Research Partners
🚨 NOMURA: THE MARKET MAY BE MISREADING THE ENTIRE AI DATA CENTER BOOM.

Big Tech is spending hundreds of billions on AI infrastructure. Free cash flow is under pressure. Investors are worried the AI boom isn't profitable.

But Nomura argues something very different:

AI infrastructure is already highly profitable. The cash flows simply haven't caught up with the investment cycle.

Here's the breakdown 🧵👇

1/ The profitability numbers tell a different story.

According to Nomura's November 2 report:

• AWS revenue: $46B, +39% YoY
• AWS operating margin: 38.7%
• Google Cloud revenue: $30.7B, +103% YoY
• Google Cloud operating margin: 36.2%
• Azure growth: +48%

These are not the numbers of an industry struggling to generate operating profits.

2/ The real issue is timing, not necessarily profitability.

Big Tech pays for data centers, GPUs, networking and memory upfront.

Revenue and cash generation arrive over subsequent years.

That creates a classic free-cash-flow J-curve:

CAPEX accelerates → FCF deteriorates → Infrastructure generates revenue → Investment growth moderates → FCF recovers.

3/ Nomura expects operating income to surge before free cash flow.

Its illustrative forecasts suggest operating-income growth could peak around 2029, while FCF growth accelerates later.

That distinction matters enormously for investors valuing AI infrastructure businesses.

4/ Why can't hyperscalers simply stop spending?

Because AI increasingly threatens their existing businesses.

Search, advertising, shopping, software and cloud services are being reshaped by AI agents.

Companies that underinvest today risk surrendering customers, data and market share tomorrow.

5/ Demand may not be the primary constraint. Capacity is.

Nomura cites enormous contracted cloud backlogs:

• Google Cloud: $560.8B
• AWS: ~$496B
• Microsoft commercial RPO: $677B

These figures have different reporting definitions, but collectively illustrate substantial contracted demand.

6/ Big Tech has financing alternatives to cutting CAPEX.

Nomura identifies four paths:

① Accelerate investment
② Freeze CAPEX
③ Use joint ventures and operating leases
④ Monetize contracted future cash flows
Its preferred expectation is continued investment supported by increasingly sophisticated financing structures.

7/ Oracle offers a real-world example.

Nomura highlights Oracle's combination of long-term leases, project financing, customer prepayments and customer-provided hardware.

The broader message: hyperscalers can restructure who finances infrastructure without necessarily reducing how much infrastructure gets built.

8/ This distinction is critical for semiconductors and memory.

Negative hyperscaler FCF does not automatically imply collapsing demand for GPUs, DRAM, HBM or other data-center components.

If spending continues through financing structures, semiconductor demand can remain resilient even while hyperscalers optimize their balance sheets.

9/ What could invalidate the thesis?

A genuine compute oversupply.

Watch:

• Cloud revenue growth
• GPU rental pricing
• Contracted backlog growth
• Data-center utilization
• Memory supply commitments
• Hyperscaler investment guidance

These are more useful indicators than negative FCF alone.

10/ The investment takeaway:

The key question is not simply:

"Why is Big Tech burning so much cash?"

It is:

"Will the infrastructure being built today generate enough durable cash flow to justify its cost of capital?"

Nomura is optimistic.

But the answer ultimately depends on pricing, utilization, investment discipline and the durability of AI demand.

The AI infrastructure cycle may be a cash-flow timing problem rather than a profitability crisis.

$NVDA $MU $GOOGL $MSFT $AMZN $META $ORCL

items.title: RT The Arc: 🚨 Shiprocket turned PAT positive in Q2 FY27, reporting a Rs 0.6 crore profit versus a Rs 20.3 crore loss a year ago. Revenue from opera...
items.description_html:
RT The Arc
🚨 Shiprocket turned PAT positive in Q2 FY27, reporting a Rs 0.6 crore profit versus a Rs 20.3 crore loss a year ago.

Revenue from operations rose 35% YoY to Rs 673.6 crore, while adjusted EBITDA improved to Rs 14.2 crore.

Shiprocket’s core business grew 25% YoY, while its emerging businesses grew 61% and now contribute 31% of revenue, up from 26% a year ago.

Within that, Martech grew 102% and Omnichannel grew 79%, helped by brands using Shiprocket to replenish quick-commerce dark stores.

The balance sheet has strengthened too. Shiprocket used IPO proceeds to repay all borrowings.

items.title: RT Pratik Bhakta: NPCI recorded 25.4bn UPI transactions in October. Headline figures might say a significant bump. But there is a deeper story behind ...
items.description_html:
RT Pratik Bhakta
NPCI recorded 25.4bn UPI transactions in October.

Headline figures might say a significant bump. But there is a deeper story behind the numbers.

Sep 2026 (24bn txs) was a slightly slower month for UPI, after a good August (24.5bn txns).

October has been a good recovery in that sense.

Generally UPI adds around 1 bn transactions every month if you look at the past trends.

2026:
April: 22.3 billion
May: 23.2 billion
June: 22.7 billion (was down)
July: 23.6 billion (it recovered)
Aug: 24.5 billion
Sep: 24 billion (down)
Oct: 25.4 billion (good recovery)

Market commentary on festive season sales was not that exciting, especially from listed fintechs. Diwali is next weekend followed by Bhai Dooj...so it will be interesting to see how comsumption picks up in November.

Interested to stay up with the number trends? Follow The Money should be your monthly go-to place. Link for last month's newsletter in the post below.

items.description_html:
RT Pratik Bhakta
There is an interesting trend shaping up in the credit card biz for banks.

While card distribution is going up steadily, the share of revolvers has gone down significantly.

SBI Card data shows that interest-earning receivables are down to 55% from more than 60%, two years earlier.

A Bernstein report from August also shows that the ratio of outstanding balances to spends has gone down to 12% from 21% in the last decade.

Snapshot below shows the value outstanding for credit cards has almost remained flat between August 2026 and 2025.

items.title: RT Pratik Bhakta: Some imp takeaways from the PB Fintech Q2FY27 results: Most of the conversations were around regulations and its potential impact on...
items.description_html:
RT Pratik Bhakta
Some imp takeaways from the PB Fintech Q2FY27 results:

Most of the conversations were around regulations and its potential impact on the business.

1. If regulations around broker commissions come out as suggested, Policybazaar's POSP business in its current form might become unviable.

2. PB Fintech will push harder on the non-insurance biz lines to continue stability in revenues, as core insurance broking revenue will be impacted.

3. Company not evaluating any plans around taking any minority stake in any insurance manufacturer.

4. It might evaluate a manufacturing role in the future since PB is a distributor with the heart of a manufacturer.

5. This year, in terms of demand for insurance products, was tough..so the company had to step up its marketing spends to push for biz growth.
